Blank verse. Unrhymed poetry written in iambic pentameter, a rhythmic pattern of unstressed and stressed syllables—da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM—repeated five times per line. Pioneered in English by poets of the English Renaissance, particularly Christopher Marlowe and William Shakespeare, blank verse became the dominant form for serious dramatic and narrative poetry.

Iambic pentameter consists of five iambs, metrical feet of two syllables with unstressed followed by stressed. The blank refers to the absence of rhyme. The regularity comes from meter, not end-rhyme. Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey introduced this form to English in the sixteenth century, adapting the Italian verso sciolto.

Christopher Marlowe popularized blank verse for drama in plays like Tamburlaine and Doctor Faustus, proving it could match the energy and passion of spoken dialogue. William Shakespeare mastered it, using blank verse as the foundation for his dramatic verse while varying the meter for dramatic effect—speeding lines for excitement, slowing them for melancholy. John Milton later elevated blank verse to epic grandeur in Paradise Lost, demonstrating that unrhymed verse could sustain philosophical and narrative complexity at the highest level.

Blank verse offers a middle path between prose and rhymed poetry. It's more naturalistic than rhyme but more elevated and patterned than free verse. Modern poets rarely write in strict blank verse now, though the form remains important in understanding English literary tradition, prosody, and dramatic verse technique.
